quote: Awesome. Yeah. Because I got me and my bunch of my neighbors, that were installed. We were gonna go with, you know, Aurora solar or something like that. But, apparently, they just filed bankruptcy.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a prior competitive relationship (Freedom Pro, formerly considering Aurora) that collapsed due to bankruptcy. The rep acknowledges sympathetically but never probes what was previously quoted, what system size was discussed, or what the neighbors' experience was — competitive intel the closer could use.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged this out of setter scope and deliberately left it for the closer to dig into during the full proposal conversation.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask one quick follow-up ('what size system were they proposing, and did you get a design?') — costs 15 seconds and hands the closer real comparison data.

quote: the way the programs work is you need to be the homeowner, which I have you here as. Was there anyone else on the side of the home with you?
stewart_read: The rep's own CRM/lead record apparently lists the customer as the homeowner, but this is about to be contradicted by the customer's next line. This is the root of the ownership confusion that persists through the rest of the call — the rep is working from a bad data assumption and never fully corrects course.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have simply misspoken and the record is accurate, with the customer's later self-contradiction being the real source of ambiguity rather than the rep's data.
coaching_implication: When the lead record and the customer's live statement conflict, the rep should pause and explicitly reconcile it in the moment rather than letting both versions stand unresolved.

quote: Yeah. So it's gonna be under my my mom and dad's name. I live here with them, so the the entire program will be under their name.
stewart_read: This is not the standard spouse/adult-child-on-title protocol (which assumes the homeowner is on the call and a co-decider needs to join) — here it is inverted: the person on the call is NOT the homeowner, and the actual homeowners (parents) are not on the call at all. This is a schema gap Ion should clarify: does the setter book with a non-owner household member and let the closer sort ownership, or does the setter need the actual titleholder on the appointment before booking?
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be following an implicit norm (common on this floor) that any adult household member can gather initial info and the closer confirms ownership before proceeding, making this a non-issue by design.
coaching_implication: Flag for Kenny: when the caller admits the home is titled to someone else entirely (not a spouse, an adult non-present relative), does policy require getting that owner on the appointment before booking? Right now the appointment is set with only the non-owner customer confirmed.

quote: Yeah. So it's gonna be me making a decision. I mean, technically, it is my house. So that's why I'm the one that's the decision maker.
stewart_read: The customer now reverses his own 02:03 statement, claiming ownership and sole decision authority. The rep says only 'Okay' and proceeds to booking without reconciling this with the earlier 'it's under my mom and dad's name' statement — a second, distinct touch on the same unresolved ownership question.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged this contradiction as not worth relitigating mid-call since the customer had already asserted control, choosing to keep momentum toward booking rather than re-opening the ownership question.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to say something like 'just to make sure the appointment is set up right — are you and your parents on the title together, or is it fully in their name?' before booking, so the closer isn't surprised.

stewart_read: Customer hands over a specific kWh usage figure (1348) unprompted and clearly. The rep acknowledges with 'Okay. Okay.' and moves straight into a residency-length question rather than reflecting the number back or connecting it to potential savings/curiosity about the upcoming design.
alternative_hypothesis: Because this is usage in kWh rather than a dollar bill amount, and the rep's job here is data capture for the design (not persuasion), the rep may be correctly staying in scope by not editorializing on the number.
coaching_implication: Encourage a light reflect-back ('1348 kWh, got it — that'll give the design team a solid number to work the savings off of') to keep the bill/usage figure alive as a hook heading into the appointment.

quote: Okay. And do you see what you have? I have a Tesla phone. I have a Tesla, so it's gonna be a little bit more.
stewart_read: The transcript is garbled here ('Tesla phone... I have a Tesla'), so it's unclear whether the customer is referencing an EV, some other device, or a transcription artifact. If it is an EV, that materially raises the household's electric load and would be a strong anchor for system sizing — but given the ambiguity, this should be treated as a possible signal rather than a confirmed one.
alternative_hypothesis: This may simply be a transcription/audio artifact with no real informational content, in which case there was nothing concrete for the rep to act on.
coaching_implication: If the audio is re-checked and confirms an EV reference, the rep should have asked a quick clarifying follow-up ('is that a Tesla vehicle you're charging at home?') to size the system correctly and use it as a forward-pulling anchor. Flag as unconfirmed pending audio review.

quote: Perfect. And I think I'll make a deal. Like I said, I got old neighbors that are warning it. So Okay. Awesome, Ken.
stewart_read: The customer references neighbors interested in solar for a second time (tied to the referral program the rep raised earlier at 01:39), but the rep does not capture names, contact info, or commit to following up on the referral before moving into scheduling logistics.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be deliberately deferring referral capture to a later touch (post-appointment) rather than derailing the booking flow in the closing seconds of the call.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to close the loop on referrals raised twice in one call — a quick 'let's grab their info after your appointment so I can get that bonus started for you' locks in the incentive and creates a second lead.

quote: Okay. Awesome, Ken. Well, I have you in our calendar for this Saturday. That's the eight Can you can you ping me as soon as you're on the way so that I know your ETA, and then I I can make sure I'm on home accordingly?
stewart_read: The rep never states the one-hour block ('I blocked off that time for an hour to ensure you don't feel rushed'), never gives the no-driving/at-a-computer instruction, and never runs the 'is that fair?' verbal handshake before the call ends — three separate button-up sub-elements are missing, not just a generic wrap-up gap.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may consider these elements optional filler once day and time are locked, especially given the customer's high engagement reduces perceived no-show risk.
coaching_implication: Drill the specific missing button-up lines: one-hour block statement, no-driving/computer instruction, and the explicit 'is that fair?' handshake — all three are absent here and are the mechanics tied to show-rate.
